g1.correct: She had learned the language and read guidebooks
accept: She had learned the language and read guidebooks
g1.label: 1. How had the narrator prepared?
g1.why: The text says she had studied Japanese for three years and read every guidebook she could find.

g2.correct: Please sit down — no help was needed
accept: Please sit down — no help was needed
g2.label: 2. What did “It’s fine” mean?
g2.why: The text says her host mother’s gentle “It’s fine” actually meant “Please sit down”.

g3.correct: She watched people instead of translating everything
accept: She watched people instead of translating everything
g3.label: 3. What changed things?
g3.why: Things changed when she stopped translating every sentence and started watching people instead.

g4.correct: With soft, polite phrases instead of direct questions
accept: With soft, polite phrases instead of direct questions
g4.label: 4. How did she ask for help?
g4.why: She asked softly, “Would you mind showing me…?”, instead of “What does this mean?”

g5.correct: An inverted if-clause — the “if” is dropped
accept: An inverted if-clause — the “if” is dropped
g5.label: 5. What structure is “Had I understood”?
g5.why: “Had I understood” means “If I had understood”: the if is dropped and had moves first.

g6.label: 6. What job does “asking” do?
g6.why: Remember + -ing (a gerund) means remembering something you did earlier.

g1.label: 1. If you ___ to a country…, you will notice
g1.why: First conditional: if + present simple, then will in the main clause.

g2.label: 2. If I had known…, I ___ such an expensive present
g2.why: Third conditional: if + past perfect, then would have + past participle.

g3.label: 3. If she ___ more attention…, she would learn
g3.why: Second conditional: if + past simple, then would + infinitive.

g4.label: 4. You will settle in faster if you ___
g4.why: First conditional: the if-clause uses the present simple, not will.

g5.label: 5. If they had warned me…, I ___ so nervous
g5.why: Third conditional: if + past perfect, then would have + past participle.

g6.label: 6. If you ___ homesick, call a friend
g6.why: If + present simple with an imperative gives advice for situations that really happen.

g7.label: 7. We ___ the festival if our host brother hadn’t explained
g7.why: Third conditional: if + past perfect (hadn’t explained), then would have + past participle.

g8.label: 8. If I could give one piece of advice, it ___ this
g8.why: Second conditional: if + past (could), then would + infinitive for an imagined situation.

g1.label: 1. ___ you mind if I sat here?
g1.why: “Would you mind if I + past simple?” is the polite way to ask permission.

g2.label: 2. Could you ___ me where…?
g2.why: Modal verbs like could are followed by the infinitive without to.

g3.label: 3. I was wondering if you ___ help me
g3.why: “I was wondering if you could…” is a very polite request; could + infinitive.

g4.label: 4. Would you mind ___ a photo of us?
g4.why: “Would you mind” is followed by the -ing form.

g5.label: 5. ___ it be all right if I came later?
g5.why: “Would it be all right if I + past simple?” politely asks permission.

g6.label: 6. Do you think you ___ speak more slowly?
g6.why: “Do you think you could…?” is a polite request; could + infinitive without to.

g7.label: 7. Could I ask you ___ the window?
g7.why: Ask someone + to-infinitive: could I ask you to open…?

g8.label: 8. Would you be so kind ___ to write…?
g8.why: The fixed polite phrase is “Would you be so kind as to…?”
